passage: Vishal was painting the new sign for his mother Rajni's tailoring shop when his father came back from the mandi. Bauji glanced at the letters, careful peacock-blue curves, and said, "Your cousin Deepak cleared the police exam. And you're painting boards." He said it the way he always did, not loudly, just tired. Vishal kept his brush steady. It was the same tone as when Bauji had called his drawing notebook a waste of paper in Class 8, the same as when he'd praised Deepak's marks at every wedding. Rajni touched Vishal's shoulder but said nothing. Vishal finished the last letter. It was good; he knew it was good. He also knew, somewhere in his stomach, that it would never count here. Not in this house, not as he was.

qa.q: What colour were the letters Vishal painted?
qa.a: They were careful peacock-blue curves.

qa.q: What belief has built up in Vishal over the years, and what shows it?
qa.a: He believes he will never be accepted as he is; even knowing the sign is good, he feels in his stomach that it will never count in this house.

qa.q: What turning point might still be open to Vishal at this stage?
qa.a: He could share the hurt with someone safe, like Rajni or a friend, and later find a calm moment to tell his father how the comparisons feel, before the wound hardens.

qa.q: What might Rajni be feeling when she touches Vishal's shoulder but says nothing?
qa.a: She seems to feel for him and want to comfort him, yet may feel unable to challenge his father openly.

grounding: A young man whose father keeps comparing him to a cousin and dismissing his art has come to believe he can never be accepted as he is.

passage: Siddiq and Thabo were sitting on the university steps in Durban when Siddiq's phone lit up. A message from Abba: a photo of his cousin Imran in a graduation gown, engineering, top of the class. No words. None were needed. Thabo leaned over. "Your dad again?" Siddiq nodded and closed his sketchbook over the half-finished drawing of the harbour cranes. "Last holiday he saw this book and asked if I was twelve." He tried to laugh. Every family dinner there was a cousin held up: Imran's marks, Yusuf's job. Siddiq stared at the cover. "Doesn't matter what I do," he said quietly. "I'll always be the wrong son." Thabo didn't argue. He just sat closer.

qa.q: What was in the photo Abba sent?
qa.a: A photo of his cousin Imran in a graduation gown.

qa.q: What does Siddiq closing his sketchbook suggest he felt when the message arrived?
qa.a: He felt hurt and small, as if his art had to be hidden; years of comparisons have made him believe he will never be accepted.

qa.q: What could help Siddiq before this hurt hardens further?
qa.a: Talking openly with a friend like Thabo, and perhaps a counsellor, could help him hold on to his worth and find words for a calm talk with his father later.

qa.q: How might Abba see the photo he sent?
qa.a: He may think he is motivating Siddiq and not realise how deeply each comparison lands, or how far it is pushing his son away.

grounding: A young man, shown yet another cousin's success by his father who mocks his sketching, feels he will always be the wrong son.

passage:
College counsellor's note, 14 October
Shankar came in today after his drawing tutor flagged that he had stopped submitting work. He is talented, his sketchbook is full of faces from the bus stop. When I asked about home, he laughed a little and said his father always asks why he can't be like his cousins in engineering. "When I showed him my first sketchbook, he asked if it was for school." He said it lightly, but he looked at the floor the whole time.
He said, "It's not one big thing. It's a thousand small ones. I'll never be what he wants."
I told him his art belongs to him, and that we can meet weekly. We booked Monday. I will also check in with Bhavna, his tutor.

qa.q: Who flagged that Shankar had stopped submitting work?
qa.a: His drawing tutor.

qa.q: What does Shankar looking at the floor suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems deeply hurt and hopeless, even though he speaks lightly, as if believing he can never be accepted.

qa.q: What turning point does the counsellor offer at this stage?
qa.a: Regular weekly meetings and the message that his art belongs to him, giving him a steady place to be heard.

qa.q: What might Shankar's father be missing about his son right now?
qa.a: He may not see how much each comparison hurts, or that his son is drawing real talent from everyday life.

grounding: Shows a counsellor's note on a young man hurt by years of his father's comparisons with cousins and dismissal of his art.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night
Family lunch at Chacha's. Ritu got into the IIT again, the second cousin this year. Papa said, "See, beta, discipline," and looked at me like I was the spare part.
Nobody asked about my exhibition. Two of my paintings are in the college corridor. I mentioned it once and Papa said, "Hobby is fine, but what is the plan?"
The plan. It's always the plan.
I keep a list, stupidly. Age twelve: my comic called "time-waste". Age fifteen: art class dropped for coaching. Now this. When I add them up it feels like proof. I'm not the son he wanted, and I'm tired of trying to become him.
I didn't eat dessert. Came home and painted till two.
Akash

qa.q: Where are two of Akash's paintings?
qa.a: In the college corridor.

qa.q: What does Akash's list suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels hurt and hopeless, as if the many small dismissals add up to proof he'll never be accepted.

qa.q: What turning point or support could help Akash at this stage?
qa.a: Talking with someone he trusts, like a friend or counsellor, about the hurt instead of only adding to the list.

qa.q: What might Ritu experience at this lunch?
qa.a: Ritu may feel awkward being used as the comparison, even while being praised.

grounding: Shows a young man's diary listing years of his father's comparisons with cousins and dismissal of his art, building a belief he can't be accepted.

passage: In Jorhat, at the tea stall outside his father's hardware shop, Kiran sketched the evening crowd on the back of a bill book. His father came out, glanced at it and said, "Your cousin Pritam cleared his bank exam. And you draw tea glasses." He went back inside. Kiran closed the book slowly. It was the same sentence in a hundred shapes. At ten: "Look at Pritam's marks." At fifteen, when he won the district art prize: "Prizes don't feed families." Now, at twenty, he had stopped showing anyone. His friend Tanvir, sipping tea beside him, said, "Your drawing is good, you know." Kiran shrugged. Inside, an old belief had set hard: whatever he became, it would never be enough for Baba.

qa.q: What had Pritam cleared?
qa.a: His bank exam.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel after years of these comments?
qa.a: Kiran feels hurt and hopeless, believing that nothing he becomes will ever be enough for Baba.

qa.q: What small step could Kiran take at this stage, before the hurt becomes a break?
qa.a: He could tell Baba calmly, perhaps with help from Tanvir or a trusted elder, how the comparisons feel, instead of silently giving up.

qa.q: What might Baba believe he is doing with these comparisons?
qa.a: Baba may think he is pushing Kiran towards security and a steady job, without seeing how much the dismissals wound him.

grounding: Shows a young man whose father has long compared him with a cousin and dismissed his art, building a belief that he can never be accepted.
